source.title: Mathematics Part I
source.edition: Textbook for Class XII Part I, Reprint 2026-27

chapter.name: Matrices
chapter.blurb: Matrices as ordered rectangular arrays of numbers or functions: their order and elements, the types of matrices (row, column, square, diagonal, scalar, identity, zero) and equality of matrices. The chapter then develops addition, scalar multiplication and multiplication of matrices with their properties, including the non-commutativity of multiplication, and introduces the transpose, symmetric and skew symmetric matrices, and the definition and uniqueness of the inverse of a square matrix.

scope_in.item: Define a matrix as an ordered rectangular array of numbers or functions and identify its rows, columns and elements; use a matrix to record tabular data (notebooks and pens, factory workers) or the vertices of a figure
State the order m x n of a matrix, locate the element a_ij in row i and column j, count elements as mn, and list all possible orders for a given number of elements
Construct a matrix of a given order from a rule for a_ij such as a_ij = (1/2)|i - 3j|
Recognise column, row and square matrices, the diagonal of a square matrix, and diagonal, scalar, identity (I_n) and zero (O) matrices
Decide whether two matrices are equal (same order and equal corresponding elements) and equate corresponding elements to find unknowns
Add and subtract matrices of the same order, multiply a matrix by a scalar, form -A, and recognise when A + B is not defined

Use the properties of matrix addition (commutative, associative, additive identity O, additive inverse -A) and of scalar multiplication (k(A + B) = kA + kB, (k + l)A = kA + lA) to solve equations such as 2A + 3X = 5B or X + Y, X - Y given
Decide when AB is defined, find its order, and compute products of matrices (including row times column), including real-life cost and revenue problems

Recognise that matrix multiplication is not commutative, that AB may be defined when BA is not, and that a product of two non-zero matrices can be the zero matrix; diagonal matrices of the same order commute
Use the associative and distributive laws and the identity IA = AI = A; compute powers A^2, A^3 and polynomial expressions such as A^2 - 5A + 7I
Find the transpose A^T (A') of a matrix and use (A^T)^T = A, (kA)^T = kA^T, (A + B)^T = A^T + B^T and (AB)^T = B^T A^T

Identify symmetric (A^T = A) and skew symmetric (A^T = -A) matrices, show a skew symmetric matrix has zero diagonal, show A + A^T is symmetric and A - A^T is skew symmetric, and express a square matrix as the sum of a symmetric and a skew symmetric matrix

Define the inverse of a square matrix through AB = BA = I, verify that two given matrices are inverses, explain why a rectangular matrix has no inverse, and use uniqueness of the inverse and (AB)^(-1) = B^(-1) A^(-1)

scope_out.item: Determinants, minors, cofactors and the adjoint of a matrix
scope_out.reason: Not in this chapter; they belong to the next chapter (Determinants).

scope_out.item: Finding the inverse of a matrix by a formula, e.g. A^(-1) = (1/|A|) adj A or the 2 x 2 (ad - bc) rule
scope_out.reason: Section 3.7 (pp. 68-69) only defines the inverse, proves uniqueness and (AB)^(-1) = B^(-1) A^(-1); it gives no method for computing an inverse. Questions only verify a given inverse by multiplication.

scope_out.item: Elementary row or column operations (transformations) and finding the inverse by elementary operations
scope_out.reason: Absent from this rationalised edition: section 3.7 ends at Theorem 4 and Exercise 3.4 has a single MCQ (p. 69); no elementary-operations section exists.

scope_out.item: Solving a system of linear equations by the matrix method (X = A^(-1)B), consistency of systems
scope_out.reason: Mentioned only as motivation in 3.1 (p. 34); the method needs determinants and adjoints from the next chapter.

scope_out.item: Proving results such as A^n formulas by mathematical induction
scope_out.reason: Miscellaneous Example 23 (p. 70) uses induction, but induction is not taught in this chapter; it is excluded from questions here.

scope_out.item: Trace, rank, eigenvalues, triangular matrices, and named types such as orthogonal, idempotent, nilpotent or involutory matrices
scope_out.reason: None of these are defined anywhere in the chapter (types are only those in 3.3, pp. 39-41); A^2 = A appears once as a condition (p. 73) without a name.
The book restricts itself to matrices whose elements are real numbers or real-valued functions (Note, p. 37).

concepts.name: Matrix, order and elements
concepts.description: A matrix as an ordered rectangular array; its rows, columns and order m x n; the element a_ij; the number of elements mn and the possible orders for a given number of elements; constructing a matrix from a rule for a_ij.
concepts.idea: A matrix is an ordered rectangular array of numbers or functions; the horizontal lines of elements are its rows and the vertical lines are its columns.
concepts.rule: A matrix with m rows and n columns has order m x n and contains mn elements; a_ij is the element in the i-th row and j-th column, with 1 <= i <= m and 1 <= j <= n.
concepts.example: A = [[30, 25], [25, 31], [27, 26]] (rows listed) records men and women workers in factories I, II, III; it is a 3 x 2 matrix with 6 elements, and a_32 = 26 is the number of women workers in factory III.

concepts.name: Types of matrices
concepts.description: Column, row and square matrices; the diagonal of a square matrix; diagonal, scalar, identity and zero matrices.
concepts.idea: Matrices are named by their shape (one column, one row, as many rows as columns) and by the pattern of their entries (zeros off the diagonal, equal diagonal entries, all ones on the diagonal, all zeros).
concepts.rule: Column matrix: m x 1. Row matrix: 1 x n. Square matrix: m = n, with diagonal a_11, a_22, ..., a_nn. Diagonal matrix: square with b_ij = 0 when i is not equal to j. Scalar matrix: diagonal with every diagonal element equal to the same k. Identity matrix I_n: diagonal elements 1, all others 0. Zero matrix O: every element 0.
concepts.example: [[3, 0, 0], [0, 3, 0], [0, 0, 3]] is a scalar matrix (so also diagonal and square); [[1, 0], [0, 1]] is I_2; [[0, 0, 0], [0, 0, 0]] is a 2 x 3 zero matrix, which is not square.

concepts.name: Equality of matrices
concepts.description: Two matrices are equal exactly when they have the same order and all corresponding elements are equal; using this to find unknowns.
concepts.idea: Equal matrices must match in shape first and then match entry by entry; the same numbers in a different arrangement do not make two matrices equal.
concepts.rule: A = [a_ij] and B = [b_ij] are equal if (i) they are of the same order and (ii) a_ij = b_ij for all i and j. Equating corresponding elements gives equations for any unknowns.

concepts.name: Addition, scalar multiplication and difference of matrices
concepts.description: Adding and subtracting matrices of the same order, multiplying a matrix by a scalar, the negative of a matrix, and the properties of these operations, including solving matrix equations such as 2A + 3X = 5B.
concepts.idea: Matrices of the same order combine entry by entry, and a scalar multiplies every entry; these operations behave like ordinary addition and multiplication of numbers.
concepts.rule: For A = [a_ij], B = [b_ij] of the same order: A + B = [a_ij + b_ij], kA = [k a_ij], -A = (-1)A, A - B = A + (-1)B. A + B is not defined for different orders. A + B = B + A; (A + B) + C = A + (B + C); A + O = A; A + (-A) = O; k(A + B) = kA + kB; (k + l)A = kA + lA.

concepts.name: Multiplication of matrices
concepts.description: When the product AB is defined and its order; computing products by rows times columns; non-commutativity; a zero product of non-zero matrices; associative and distributive laws and the identity; powers such as A^2 and expressions like A^2 - 5A + 7I; real-life products.
concepts.idea: Each entry of AB is a row of A multiplied element by element with a column of B and summed, so the order of the factors matters.
concepts.rule: AB is defined only if the number of columns of A equals the number of rows of B. If A is m x n and B is n x p, AB is m x p with c_ik = a_i1 b_1k + a_i2 b_2k + ... + a_in b_nk. In general AB is not equal to BA; AB = O is possible with A and B non-zero; (AB)C = A(BC); A(B + C) = AB + AC; (A + B)C = AC + BC; IA = AI = A.
concepts.example: Requirements [[2, 5], [8, 10]] times prices [[5], [50]] gives [[2 x 5 + 5 x 50], [8 x 5 + 10 x 50]] = [[260], [540]], the money Meera and Nadeem need.

concepts.name: Transpose of a matrix
concepts.description: The transpose A^T (also written A') obtained by interchanging rows and columns, its order, and the properties (A^T)^T = A, (kA)^T = kA^T, (A + B)^T = A^T + B^T and (AB)^T = B^T A^T.
concepts.idea: Transposing turns each row of a matrix into the corresponding column, so an m x n matrix becomes n x m.
concepts.rule: If A = [a_ij] is m x n, then A^T = [a_ji] is n x m. (A^T)^T = A; (kA)^T = kA^T; (A + B)^T = A^T + B^T; (AB)^T = B^T A^T (the order is reversed).

concepts.name: Symmetric and skew symmetric matrices
concepts.description: Symmetric (A^T = A) and skew symmetric (A^T = -A) matrices, zero diagonal of a skew symmetric matrix, A + A^T symmetric and A - A^T skew symmetric, and expressing any square matrix as the sum of a symmetric and a skew symmetric matrix.
concepts.idea: In a symmetric matrix the entries mirror each other across the diagonal; in a skew symmetric matrix the mirrored entries are negatives of each other and the diagonal is all zero.
concepts.rule: A square matrix A is symmetric if A^T = A (a_ij = a_ji) and skew symmetric if A^T = -A (a_ji = -a_ij), which forces every a_ii = 0. For any square A, A + A^T is symmetric, A - A^T is skew symmetric, and A = (1/2)(A + A^T) + (1/2)(A - A^T).

concepts.name: Invertible matrices
concepts.description: The inverse of a square matrix defined by AB = BA = I; verifying that two matrices are inverses; rectangular matrices have no inverse; uniqueness of the inverse; (AB)^(-1) = B^(-1) A^(-1).
concepts.idea: B undoes A when multiplying them in either order gives the identity matrix; only square matrices can have such a partner.
concepts.rule: If A is square of order m and a square matrix B of order m satisfies AB = BA = I, then B = A^(-1) and A is invertible; then A is also the inverse of B. A rectangular matrix has no inverse. The inverse, if it exists, is unique. If A and B are invertible of the same order, (AB)^(-1) = B^(-1) A^(-1).
